l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The Boeotians fought the Lacedemonians and their allies and were also attacked by Alexander’s cavalry in Thessaly. When their allies deserted them and provisions ran short, Epaminondas rescued their army during its retreat.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The Thebans refused the peace conditions proposed by Philiscus because they had brought all Boeotia under their own government. They sent eight thousand heavy-armed men and six hundred horse into Thessaly after Pelopidas and Ismenias were imprisoned.

l: Pelopidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Pelopidas went to Thessaly with Ismenias to enlarge Theban power beyond the Peloponnesus. Alexander, tyrant of Pherae, unexpectedly seized and imprisoned him, but Epaminondas later helped free him.

l: Ismenias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Ismenias, a close friend of Pelopidas and a man esteemed for his courage, accompanied Pelopidas to Thessaly. Alexander, tyrant of Pherae, seized and imprisoned them both.

l: Alexander of Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Alexander imprisoned Pelopidas and Ismenias, then fought the Boeotians in Thessaly with support from the Athenians and other allies. His cavalry attacked the Boeotian army during its retreat, but Epaminondas repulsed the attack and brought the army safely away. Alexander later massacred the inhabitants of Scotussa after surrounding them at a common assembly.

l: Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Pherae was ruled by Alexander, who imprisoned Pelopidas and Ismenias and later received opposition from Epaminondas’s forces. The text also identifies Alexander as the tyrant of Pherae.

l: Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Thessaly was the region where Pelopidas and Ismenias were seized and imprisoned by Alexander, tyrant of Pherae. The Thebans entered Thessaly with an army, and Epaminondas later helped secure Pelopidas’s release.

l: Epaminondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Epaminondas was serving as a private soldier when the Boeotian army chose him as its general during a desperate retreat in Thessaly. He placed light-armed troops and cavalry in the rear, repulsed Alexander’s forces, and safely brought off the army. He later invaded the Peloponnesus and helped free Pelopidas.

l: Arcadians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The Arcadians were defeated by the Lacedemonians in a battle in which more than ten thousand Arcadians were said to have been slain. Fearing the Lacedemonians afterward, they founded Megalopolis and settled people from several Arcadian communities there.

l: Megalopolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Megalopolis was founded by the Arcadians after their defeat by the Lacedemonians. It was placed in a location suited for security and populated with Menalians and Parrhasians from twenty villages.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The Carthaginians were weakened by plague and the defection of many Africans when Dionysius attacked their territory in Sicily. They later manned two hundred ships, unexpectedly entered the harbor at Eryx, and carried away most of Dionysius’s ships.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Sicily was ruled by Dionysius the tyrant, who launched an invasion of Carthaginian territory from there. Dionysius died in Sicily after excessive drinking and feasting, and his son Dionysius the younger succeeded him.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Syracuse was the seat of Dionysius the tyrant and the place to which he sent ships after reducing his fleet at Eryx. The singer who brought news of Dionysius’s victory in Athens arrived at Syracuse and received a reward.

l: Dionysius the younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Dionysius the younger succeeded his father as ruler after Dionysius the tyrant died. He called a senate, sought the people’s goodwill, conducted his father’s funeral with great ceremony, and arranged affairs to secure his throne.

l: Cos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The people of Coos settled in the city they afterward occupied and made it populous and prosperous. They surrounded it with a large wall, furnished it with an excellent harbor, and increased its public revenues and private wealth.

l: Persian king, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The Persian king sent ambassadors to persuade the Grecians to end their disputes. His mediation brought the Laconic and Boeotian War to an end.

l: Laconic and Boeotian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The Laconic and Boeotian War had continued for more than five years from the Battle of Leuctra. It ended when the Persian king sent ambassadors to persuade the Grecians to agree and set aside their animosities.

l: Battle between the Lacedaemonians and Arcadians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The battle ended in a decisive victory for the Lacedaemonians, with more than ten thousand Arcadians slain and no Lacedaemonian reported lost. It was the first considerable Lacedaemonian success since the Battle of Leuctra.

l: Epaminondas’s rescue of the Boeotian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: During the Boeotian retreat through the plain of Thessaly, Alexander’s cavalry attacked the army’s rear while the troops lacked food and were unable to advance or hold their ground. Although serving as a private soldier, Epaminondas was chosen general, organized the rear guard, repulsed the attackers, and brought the army safely away.

l: Dionysius’s Sicilian war against Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Dionysius attacked Carthaginian territory with thirty thousand foot, three thousand horse, and three hundred ships, taking Selinus, Entella, and Eryx and besieging Lilybaeum. He raised the siege when the garrison resisted, then lost most of the ships stationed at Eryx after the Carthaginians unexpectedly entered the harbor.

l: Dionysius’s death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Dionysius died after ruling for thirty-eight years. He became violently ill after excessive feasting and drinking to celebrate news that his tragedy had won a victory at Athens, a result connected in the text with an oracle that he would die after overcoming those better than himself.

l: Alexander’s massacre at Scotussa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Alexander, tyrant of Pherae, held a grudge against the people of Scotussa in Thessaly. He summoned them to a common assembly, surrounded them with his guard, killed them all, threw their bodies into the ditches beyond the walls, and plundered the city.

l: Epaminondas’s invasion of the Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: Epaminondas entered the Peloponnesus with all his forces, joined by the Achaians and other allies. He restored Dymon, Naupactus, and Calydon to their ancient liberties before making another expedition into Thessaly.

l: Coos’s fortification and settlement, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIIL
s: The people of Coos settled in their later city, increased its population, and enclosed it with a costly large wall. They also provided it with an excellent harbor, after which the city grew in public revenues and private wealth.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Arcadian exiles seized Lassia in Triphylia, leading to war between the Arcadians and Elians, in which the Elians were defeated near Lassia and the Arcadians captured several cities. The Pisates, aided by the Arcadians, took control of the 104th Olympiad and conducted the Olympic games, though the Elians rejected that Olympiad as unlawful. Epaminondas persuaded the Thebans to seek dominion of the sea, and Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium were brought under Theban obedience, while the Thebans later destroyed Orchomenus after uncovering a conspiracy. The Thessalians sought Theban aid against Alexander of Pherae; Pelopidas won a victory but was killed, and the text praises his services to Thebes, including the recovery of Cadmea and victories over the Lacedaemonians.

l: Arcadian exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Arcadian exiles made an excursion out of Elis and seized Lassia, a strong castle in Triphylia. The Elians later came to their assistance when the Arcadians besieged Lassia.

l: Elis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Elis disputed possession of Triphylia with the Arcadians. Its forces were defeated near Lassia, after which the Arcadians marched into Elis and captured several cities.

l: Triphylia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Triphylia was disputed for a long time by the Arcadians and Elians, with possession changing between them. Lassia was identified as a strong castle in Triphylia.

l: Lassia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Lassia was seized by Arcadian exiles and later besieged by the Arcadians. The Elians fought near it in an unsuccessful attempt to assist the exiles.

l: Arcadians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Arcadians recovered Lassia after the Elians had dispossessed them, with Athenian support in the war. After victory near Lassia, they invaded Elis and captured Marganus, Cropium, Cyparissia, and Coryphasium.

l: Elians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Elians dispossessed the Arcadians from Lassia under the shelter and colour of the Arcadian fugitives. They were defeated near Lassia and later opposed the Pisates and Arcadians at the Olympic games.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Athenians joined the Arcadians in the war against the Elians. Later, the Athenian general Laches attempted with a strong fleet to obstruct Theban designs at sea but was forced to sail back.

l: battle near Lassia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The battle near Lassia was fought between the Elians and forces supporting the Arcadians. The Elians were routed because they were overpowered by numbers and lost more than two hundred men.

l: 104th Olympiad, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The 104th Olympiad was celebrated by the Pisates and Arcadians, with Phocides of Athens victorious. The Elians did not count this Olympiad in their annals because they considered it forced and unlawful.

l: Pisates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Pisates claimed the right to convene and manage the Olympic games based on old traditions. With Arcadian assistance, they defeated the Elians and managed the sports at the 104th Olympiad.

l: Olympic Games, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Olympic games became the subject of a dispute between the Pisates and Elians. The Pisates and Arcadians fought the Elians during the celebration, while the assembled Greeks watched as spectators.

l: Epaminondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Epaminondas persuaded the Thebans to seek dominion of the sea, arguing that their land power would make maritime supremacy attainable. He was sent with forces to Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium, frightened the Athenian general Laches into withdrawing, and brought those cities under Theban obedience before later being killed at Mantinea.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Thebans resolved to build a hundred galleys and as many docks in order to gain dominion of the sea. They brought Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium under their obedience, destroyed Orchomenus after a conspiracy, and later sent aid to the Thessalians under Pelopidas.

l: dominion of the sea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Epaminondas urged the Thebans to gain dominion of the sea, arguing that their sovereignty on land would help them become masters at sea. The Thebans decreed the construction of a hundred galleys and docks and sought assistance from Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium.

l: Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Rhodes was asked to assist the Thebans in building a fleet and docks. Epaminondas later brought Rhodes under the obedience of Thebes.

l: Chios, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Chios was asked to assist the Thebans in preparing their fleet and docks. Epaminondas later brought Chios under the obedience of Thebes.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Byzantium was asked to assist the Thebans in preparing their fleet and docks. Epaminondas later brought Byzantium under the obedience of Thebes.

l: Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Mantinea was the site of the battle in which Epaminondas was killed. He obtained a famous victory there for his country by his own fall.

l: Theban invasion of Orchomenus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Theban invasion of Orchomenus followed the discovery of a conspiracy involving Theban fugitives and three hundred horsemen from Orchomenus. The Thebans captured the city, killed all the men, and sold the women and children as slaves.

l: Orchomenus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Three hundred horsemen of Orchomenus joined Theban fugitives in a plan to change the government of Thebes. After the conspiracy was exposed, the city was captured and razed, its men were killed, and its women and children were sold as slaves.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Boeotians learned of the conspiracy involving the Orchomenian horsemen after some conspirators betrayed their fellows. They later held a general council and ordered Pelopidas to assist the Thessalians with seven thousand men.

l: Alexander of Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Alexander of Pherae fought the Thessalians and defeated them repeatedly before Pelopidas arrived. He held the higher ground and initially prevailed, but after further defeat he was forced to make peace, restore captured towns, deliver Magnesia and Phthiotis to the Boeotians, and retain only Pherae.

l: Thessalians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Thessalians made war upon Alexander of Pherae but were often beaten and lost many men. They solicited Theban assistance under Pelopidas, and after Alexander's defeat received the return of the towns he had taken.

l: Pelopidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Pelopidas led seven thousand men to assist the Thessalians against Alexander of Pherae. He won a victory after personally charging Alexander's forces but died from numerous wounds; the text praises his services in freeing Thebes, defeating the Lacedaemonians, helping rebuild Messenia, and extending Theban power.

l: Cadmea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: Pelopidas was generally credited with freeing Thebes after the exiles recovered the citadel of Cadmea. The recovery of Cadmea was described as the chief cause of the later advantages and successes of the Thebans.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX,
s: The Lacedaemonians were defeated by Pelopidas at Tegea, where the Thebans first erected a trophy over them. At Leuctra, Pelopidas led the Sacred Band and was the first to break into the Lacedaemonian forces; he later erected another trophy after defeating them near Sparta.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Arcadians divided between the Tegeans and Mantineans, leading the Tegeans to seek Boeotian aid and the Mantineans to seek Athenian and Lacedaemonian support. Epaminondas led the Boeotian alliance, attempted unsuccessfully to surprise Sparta, and then fought the allied forces at Mantinea. The Boeotians routed the Lacedaemonians after Epaminondas killed their general, but Epaminondas was mortally wounded and died after learning that his side had won. The exhausted Greeks then ended the war through a general offensive and defensive league, although the Lacedaemonians refused to join because of their hostility toward the Messenians.

l: Arcadians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Arcadians divided into factions led by the Tegeans and Mantineans. They fought among themselves and participated in the conflict surrounding Mantinea.

l: Mantineans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Mantineans promoted war against the Elians because they feared being called to account for sacred objects they had taken and profaned. They sought Athenian and Lacedaemonian assistance, fought at Mantinea, and were routed by the Boeotian and Thessalian horsemen.

l: Tegeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Tegeans led one of the Arcadian factions and sent an ambassador to the Boeotians for assistance. They were supported by Epaminondas and the Boeotian alliance in the war against the Mantineans.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Boeotians appointed Epaminondas general and sent him with a strong army to aid the Tegeans. Their forces defeated the Lacedaemonians at Mantinea, although Epaminondas was mortally wounded in the victory.

l: Epaminondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Epaminondas commanded the Boeotian forces, attempted to surprise Sparta, and later marched against Mantinea. At the battle of Mantinea he personally charged the Lacedaemonians, killed their general, and broke their division, but he received a mortal wound and died after learning that his side had won. The text praises his military skill, courage, justice, contempt for wealth, and other virtues.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Athenians joined the Mantineans and Lacedaemonians and sent six thousand auxiliaries into Mantinea. Their horse were defeated by the Theban horse, though the Athenian left wing's losses were partly repaired by the Eleian horsemen.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Lacedaemonians allied with the Mantineans and Athenians, invaded Arcadia, and defended Sparta against Epaminondas. They were routed at Mantinea after Epaminondas broke their division, but they later sent a trumpet to obtain burial rights for their dead and were the only Greeks who refused to swear to the general league.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Sparta was threatened by Epaminondas, who marched against it at night while its army was away. Agis warned the city, and Agesilaus organized its defense; Epaminondas's assault failed after the Lacedaemonian army returned.

l: Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Mantinea was the city whose factional dispute helped cause the war. It was briefly left without adequate defense, but six thousand Athenian auxiliaries entered and secured it before Epaminondas could capture it.

l: Messenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Messenians were included in the general Greek league formed after the battle. The Lacedaemonians refused the peace articles because of their implacable hatred of the Messenians.

l: battle of Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The battle involved the Mantineans, Lacedaemonians, Elians, Athenians, and allies against the Tegeans, Boeotians, Argives, and their confederates. The Boeotians gained the advantage after Epaminondas killed the Lacedaemonian general and routed their division, but Epaminondas was mortally wounded; both sides initially claimed victory and erected trophies before the dead were buried.

l: general Greek league, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: After the battle, the war-weary Greeks formed a general offensive and defensive league that included the Messenians. The Lacedaemonians alone refused to swear to its articles because of their hostility toward the Messenians.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The unit describes a Persian revolt, Tachos's war against Persia, and the conflict between Tachos and his son Nectanabis for control of Egypt. Orontes and other Persian rebels betray their allies, while Datames defeats treacherous forces in Cappadocia before Artaxerxes arranges his death. Agesilaus helps restore Tachos after defeating the Egyptians, and later events include a civic conflict at Megalopolis, Alexander's attack on Peparethos, and Chares's abuses in Corcyra.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Artaxerxes faced revolts by governors, commanders, and coastal peoples, as well as war with Tachos and the Lacedaemonians. He accepted Tachos after Tachos fled Egypt, used him against the Egyptians, and later arranged Datames's death by ambush. He died after reigning forty-three years.

l: Tachos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Tachos, king of Egypt, declared war against the Persians and assembled a fleet, Egyptian infantry, and Greek mercenaries with Lacedaemonian support. After Nectanabis revolted and took Egypt, Tachos fled to Artaxerxes, who forgave him and made him general against the Egyptians. Tachos was restored to his kingdom after Agesilaus defeated Nectanabis's forces.

l: Orontes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Orontes, governor of Mysia, joined the Persian revolt and was made general of the rebel army. After receiving money to pay twenty thousand soldiers, he betrayed the rebels, seized those who brought him the money, and delivered cities and soldiers to the king's lieutenants.

l: Datames, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Datames, governor of Cappadocia, opposed Artabazus with cavalry and twenty thousand mercenary infantry. After Mithrobarzanes betrayed him, Datames pursued the deserters and defeated the forces involved, killing or capturing many of them. Artaxerxes later had Datames killed in an ambush.

l: Agesilaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Agesilaus commanded Tachos's ten thousand Greek mercenaries and advised Tachos to remain in Egypt. He helped Tachos escape an Egyptian siege, defeated the Egyptians in a position protected by water, and thereby restored Tachos to Egypt. He later died at Cyrene while returning to Sparta.

l: Nectanabis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Nectanabis, Tachos's son, participated in the revolt against his father and drew Egyptian commanders and soldiers to his side with gifts and promises. He took control of Egypt and led more than one hundred thousand men against Tachos, but his forces were defeated by Agesilaus.

l: Chares, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Chares replaced Leosthenes as Athenian commander and was sent with a fleet against Alexander. He spent his time frightening the enemy and oppressing allies, especially at Corcyra, where his actions caused sedition, slaughter, plunder, and damage to Athenian reputation.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Persians faced a widespread revolt among Asian coastal peoples, provincial governors, and commanders. They also fought Tachos and later received Tachos after he fled Egypt.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Lacedaemonians joined Tachos against Persia and sent Agesilaus with one thousand men to aid the Egyptians. They opposed Artaxerxes because he had ordered the Messenians to be included in the public league of the Greeks.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Greeks served as mercenaries in Tachos's Egyptian campaign. Greek soldiers under Agesilaus helped defeat the Egyptians and restore Tachos.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Egyptians, led by Nectanabis after Tachos fled, besieged Tachos and Agesilaus in a city and later pursued them. Their superior numbers were ineffective in the restricted ground selected by Agesilaus, and they were defeated.

l: Arcadians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Arcadians made a general peace after the battle of Mantinea but soon resumed conflict. The Arcadians were drawn into the dispute between Megalopolis and neighboring towns.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Athenians sent three thousand heavy-armed men and three hundred horse under Pammenes to support Megalopolis. They also supported Peparethos, but Alexander defeated an Athenian force at Panormus. The Athenians condemned Leosthenes and appointed Chares in his place.

l: rebels (Persian revolt), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Persian rebels included coastal peoples, governors, commanders, and allied rulers in Asia. They made Orontes general, but he betrayed them, while Rheomithres later seized revolted lords and officers and sent them to the Persian king.

l: mercenaries (Egyptian campaign), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Tachos assembled ten thousand Greek mercenaries for his campaign against Persia. Agesilaus received command of them, and they helped him escape the Egyptian siege and defeat the Egyptian army.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: In Asia, coastal peoples and several governors and commanders revolted against Artaxerxes. The revolt deprived the Persian king of half his revenues and involved Phrygia, Caria, Mysia, Lydia, and other coastal regions.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Persia was threatened by revolts in Asia and by Tachos's attack from Egypt. Artaxerxes responded by raising forces, accepting Tachos after his flight, and using him in the campaign against Egypt.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Egypt became the center of a succession conflict between Tachos and Nectanabis. Nectanabis seized the kingdom while Tachos was campaigning in Phoenicia, but Tachos later regained Egypt with Agesilaus's help.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Greece supplied soldiers for Tachos's campaign and remained involved in disputes after the battle of Mantinea. Athens intervened in the Megalopolitan conflict and in the struggle over Peparethos.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: In the Peloponnesus, the peace made after Mantinea lasted scarcely a year before Arcadian communities resumed conflict. The dispute centered on whether neighboring towns should remain incorporated into Megalopolis.

l: Megalopolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Megalopolis faced a conflict with neighboring towns that had been forced to settle there and later returned to their former homes. The Megalopolitans sought Athenian aid, and Pammenes compelled the towns to return to Megalopolis.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Athens sent forces under Pammenes to support Megalopolis and later sent a fleet under Chares after Alexander defeated Leosthenes. Athens condemned Leosthenes, confiscated his property, and appointed Chares as commander.

l: Peparethos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Peparethos was besieged by Alexander of Pherae. An Athenian garrison under Leosthenes relieved the city, but Alexander later captured one Peparethian galley and six hundred prisoners during his victory at Panormus.

l: Persian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Persian revolt spread among coastal peoples, provincial governors, and commanders who opposed Artaxerxes. Its leaders suffered repeated betrayals by Orontes and Rheomithres, weakening the rebellion and restoring Persian control over several cities and forces.

l: war between Persia and Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The war began when Tachos declared war against Persia and prepared ships and troops with Lacedaemonian and Greek support. Tachos later fled to Artaxerxes after Nectanabis seized Egypt, and Artaxerxes made him general against the Egyptians.

l: battle of Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: After the battle of Mantinea, a general peace was made among the Arcadians. The peace quickly broke down when neighboring towns returned to their former homes and Megalopolis attempted to force them back.

l: restoration of Tachos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Tachos was restored to Egypt after Agesilaus led his forces through the Egyptian encirclement and defeated Nectanabis's army in ground protected by water. Tachos rewarded Agesilaus with honorable gifts before dismissing him.

l: Agesilaus's victory over the Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Agesilaus defeated the Egyptians after choosing a position secured on both sides by water from the river. The Egyptian numbers gave them little advantage there, and their army was slaughtered and put to flight.

l: Megalopolitan civic conflict, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: The Megalopolitan civic conflict arose when neighboring towns returned from Megalopolis to their former settlements after the peace following Mantinea. Athens sent Pammenes, who forced the towns to return and ended the disturbance.

l: Chares's abuses in Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Chares caused seditions and tumults in Corcyra, an allied city. His actions produced slaughter, plunder, and confiscation of property and caused the Athenians to be condemned by their allies.

l: Egyptian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAR XL
s: Tachos prepared an Egyptian fleet of two hundred ships for the war against Persia. Chabrias was appointed its admiral, serving Tachos privately rather than under public authority.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: This unit introduces Philip son of Amyntas, who became king of Macedon after Perdiccas was killed fighting the Illyrians. Philip strengthened the Macedonians, defeated an Athenian force supporting Argæus, made peace with Athens, subdued the Pæones, and defeated the Illyrians under Bardyllis. The Illyrians then surrendered the Macedonian cities they held and made peace, while Philip prepared Macedon for the later expedition against Persia that his death prevented him from undertaking.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip was held hostage by the Illyrians and delivered to the Thebans, who placed him under the care of the father of Epaminondas. He later escaped, became king of Macedon after Perdiccas was killed, defeated the Athenians, Pæones, and Illyrians, and prepared to attack Persia.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Alexander succeeded Amyntas as king before Philip came to power. He is identified as the son who later conquered the Persians and inherited sufficient forces from Philip to overturn the Persian empire without needing the assistance of Philip's confederates.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Macedonians suffered a major defeat against the Illyrians, losing more than four thousand men and becoming fearful of continuing the war. Philip restored their confidence through speeches and military training, organized them into a close formation, and led them to victories against the Athenians, Pæones, and Illyrians.

l: Illyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Illyrians had subdued Amyntas and forced him to pay tribute, taking Philip as a hostage. They later invaded Macedon, fought Philip under Bardyllis, were defeated, and surrendered all the cities belonging to Macedon before making peace.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Athenians tried to restore Argæus to the Macedonian throne and sent Manlius with a force and fleet for that purpose. Philip defeated their mercenaries near Ægæ and later made peace with Athens by agreeing to abandon his claim to Amphipolis.

l: Paeones, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Pæones raided Macedon while it was weakened by war and threatened another invasion. After Philip made a temporary peace with them, he invaded following the death of their king Agis, defeated them, and brought them under Macedonian rule.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Greeks are described as voluntarily submitting to Philip through his military success and making him general of all Greece. Philip's death prevented him from leading the planned expedition into Asia with the forces promised by the Greek cities.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Macedon was under the servile yoke of the Illyrians when Philip came to the crown and was threatened by the Pæones, Illyrians, Athenians, and other rivals. Philip restored and expanded it, making it mistress of many cities and countries and the greatest kingdom in Europe.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Athens supported Argæus's attempt to regain the Macedonian throne and sent Manlius against Macedon. It later accepted Philip's peace proposals after he agreed to give up his claim to Amphipolis.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip's victories led the cities of Greece to submit voluntarily to him and appoint him general of all Greece. He also received a seat in the senate of the Amphictyons after defeating those who had robbed the temple at Delphi.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip devoted his thoughts to destroying the Persian monarchy after defeating the Illyrians, Pæones, Thracians, Scythians, and neighboring peoples. He died while preparing the expedition, but left Alexander enough forces to overturn the Persian empire.

l: Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Amphipolis was the principal object of Athenian concern in the conflict with Philip. Philip secured peace with Athens by agreeing to abandon all his claim to the city.

l: Philip’s reign in Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip reigned as king of Macedon for thirty-two years. He transformed Macedon from a kingdom subject to the Illyrians into the greatest kingdom in Europe and established authority over many cities and countries.

l: the Illyrian invasion of Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Illyrians invaded Macedon after Amyntas had been forced to pay tribute, and they defeated and killed Perdiccas in battle. The invasion left more than four thousand Macedonians dead and the survivors too fearful to continue the war until Philip took command.

l: the Athenian campaign against Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: The Athenians sent Manlius with three thousand armed men and a strong fleet to restore Argæus to the Macedonian throne. Philip defeated the mercenaries sent forward by Manlius near Ægæ and subsequently ended the conflict through a peace agreement.

l: Philip’s conquest of the Pæones, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: After hearing that Agis, king of the Pæones, had died, Philip invaded Pæonia with a considerable army. He defeated the Pæones in battle and forced them under the Macedonian yoke.

l: Philip’s war with the Illyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip raised an army of ten thousand foot and six hundred horse and invaded the Illyrian country. He defeated Bardyllis's army by attacking its front while his cavalry struck the flank and rear, then pursued the routed Illyrians.

l: the Illyrian-Macedonian peace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: After their defeat, the Illyrians sent another embassy and obtained peace. They agreed to surrender all the cities belonging to Macedon.

l: Asian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip planned an expedition against Persia after securing Macedon and defeating neighboring peoples. Although the Greek cities promised forces for the expedition, Philip died during the preparations, leaving Alexander to carry out the conquest with the forces already assembled.

l: the battle with the Illyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVI.
s: Philip's battle with the Illyrians was fought against Bardyllis, who brought ten thousand foot and five hundred horse. The fighting was prolonged and costly, but Philip's cavalry attacks and his assault on the front routed the Illyrians; more than seven thousand Illyrians were killed.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Dionysius the younger neglected military affairs, made peace with Carthage, fought carelessly against the Lucanians, and ultimately lost his Sicilian dominion. Dion fled Sicily to Corinth, gathered mercenaries, and returned with the aim of restoring liberty to Syracuse and other Sicilians. Civil war in Euboea ended in an agreement, while the Athenians fought the three-year Social War against Chios, Rhodes, Cos, and Byzantium, with Chabrias dying in a naval battle. Philip captured Amphipolis and Pydna, allied with the Olynthians, developed Philippi and its gold mines, and strengthened Macedonia through wealth and military power.

l: Dionysius the younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Dionysius the younger, tyrant of Syracuse, was described as inactive, slothful, and cowardly. He made peace with the Carthaginians, fought the Lucanians carelessly, neglected military exercises, and eventually lost his dominion.

l: Dion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Dion, brother of Hipparinus and brother-in-law of Dionysius the younger, was skilled in philosophy and regarded as the most expert soldier among the Syracusans. Fearing that Dionysius intended to kill him, he fled Sicily to Peloponnesus and Corinth, gathered forces, and returned to seek the liberty of Syracuse.

l: Andromachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Andromachus of Taurominium, father of the historian Timaeus, gathered the exiles of Naxos and settled them on Mount Taurus. He and his family remained there, and the settlement was called Taurominium.

l: Chares, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Chares commanded the Athenian land forces during the siege of Chios. He assaulted the walls and fought the garrison in the open field.

l: Chabrias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Chabrias commanded the Athenian fleet during the siege of Chios. His ship was pierced by the enemy, and he was wounded and killed while defending it after the other ships withdrew.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Philip, king of Macedonia, defeated the Illyrians, captured Amphipolis and Pydna, and made a league with the Olynthians. He enlarged Cremides and renamed it Philippi, developed its gold mines, accumulated wealth, raised mercenaries, and bribed some Grecians.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Syracusans were ruled by Dionysius the younger until Dion sought to restore their liberty. Dion was described as a noble Syracusan, a skilled philosopher, and an expert soldier.

l: Sicilians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Sicilians, along with the Syracusans, were later restored to their ancient liberties through Dion's efforts.

l: Corinthians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Corinthians were solicited by Dion to assist in recovering the liberty of Syracuse. Dion then gathered a force and prepared arms at Corinth.

l: mercenary soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Dion collected a band of mercenaries, obtained arms, and mustered a considerable force of mercenary soldiers. He transported them from Zacynthus to Sicily in two hired ships.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Athenians supported one party in the civil war in Euboea and later fought the Social War against Chios, Rhodes, Cos, and Byzantium. They also competed with Philip to gain the Olynthians as allies.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Boeotians supported one party in the civil war in Euboea. After the conflict ended, they returned home and laid down their arms.

l: Chians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Chians defected from the Athenians and were supported by the Byzantines, Rhodians, Coians, and Mausolus. They defended Chios against the Athenian siege.

l: Rhodians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Rhodians joined the Chians, Byzantines, and Coians in defecting from Athens and supporting Chios during the Social War.

l: Coians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Coians defected from the Athenians and assisted the Chians together with the Byzantines and Rhodians.

l: Byzantines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Byzantines defected from Athens, supported the Chians, and assisted them during the siege of Chios.

l: Olynthians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Olynthians were considered rich, powerful, and populous, making them valuable allies. Philip made a league with them and promised them Potidea and later gave them Pydna with its grounds and territories.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Macedonians benefited from Philip's victories, wealth, and military leadership. Philip raised the kingdom of Macedonia to greater majesty and glory than it had previously possessed.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Sicily was ruled by Dionysius the younger until Dion fled from it and later returned with mercenaries. Dion's efforts were intended to restore liberty to Sicily's Syracusans and other inhabitants.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Syracuse was governed by Dionysius the younger, who feared Dion and sought to remove him. Dion later gathered forces to recover Syracuse's liberty.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Athens was involved in the Social War and sent Chares and Chabrias against Chios. Philip treated the Athenian garrison from Potidea with civility and allowed it to return to Athens.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Dion went to Corinth after fleeing Sicily and solicited the Corinthians' aid. He gathered mercenaries and procured arms there before sailing toward Sicily.

l: Taurominium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Taurominium was founded when Andromachus settled the exiles of Naxos on Mount Taurus. The city became wealthy and prosperous, though the text says that in a later age its inhabitants were removed and a Roman colony was established.

l: Euboea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Euboea was divided by internal quarrels, with one party seeking aid from the Boeotians and the other from the Athenians. The resulting civil war caused widespread devastation before the inhabitants agreed to peace.

l: Chios, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Chios was besieged by Athenian land and naval forces during the Social War. The Chians defended it with assistance from the Byzantines, Rhodians, Coians, and Mausolus.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Macedonia was strengthened by Philip's victories over the Illyrians, captures of cities, accumulation of wealth, and recruitment of mercenaries. Philip's policies raised the kingdom's power and grandeur.

l: Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Amphipolis was attacked and captured by Philip after he was provoked by its injuries. Philip battered its walls, entered through the ruins, killed many opponents, executed his chief enemies, and spared the rest.

l: Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Amphipolis was situated advantageously in Thrace and was valuable to Philip because of its location and proximity to other places.

l: Pydna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Philip captured Pydna after taking Amphipolis. He later delivered Pydna, together with its grounds and territories, to the Olynthians.

l: Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Philip promised to give Potidea to the Olynthians, who had long desired it. After taking the city, he removed the Athenian garrison and allowed its members to return to Athens.

l: Cremides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Philip marched to Cremides, enlarged it, and increased its population.

l: Philippi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Philip renamed the enlarged city of Cremides Philippi. He also developed the nearby gold mines, which produced a yearly revenue of more than a thousand talents.

l: Social War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The Social War was fought by the Athenians for three years after the defection of the Chians, Rhodians, Coians, and Byzantines. Chares and Chabrias led the Athenian forces against Chios, where Chabrias was killed in a naval engagement.

l: civil war in Euboea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The civil war in Euboea began when rival parties sought assistance from the Boeotians and Athenians. Although there were many skirmishes, no great battle occurred, and the war ended in peace after the island had been devastated.

l: capture of Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The capture of Amphipolis was carried out by Philip through repeated assaults and battering rams. He entered through a breach, killed many who resisted, executed his principal enemies, and spared the rest.

l: capture of Pydna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The capture of Pydna followed Philip's capture of Amphipolis. Philip subsequently gave Pydna and its territories to the Olynthians.

l: tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: The tyranny of Syracuse was represented by Dionysius the younger, whose sloth and neglect of military affairs weakened his position. Dion's opposition to the tyranny led him to flee, gather mercenaries, and seek its overthrow.

l: Syracuse's liberty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. 11.
s: Syracuse's liberty was the goal of Dion's appeal to the Corinthians and his expedition from Zacynthus to Sicily. The text says that Dion's efforts restored the Syracusans and other Sicilians to their ancient liberties.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dion landed in Sicily with a small force, gathered supporters, and entered Syracuse after the Syracusans chose him and Megacles as generals with absolute power. The Syracusans celebrated their liberation from Dionysius, but Dionysius soon returned, deceived them with negotiations, and attacked the wall from sea to sea. Dion defeated the Dionysian forces at the wall, after which Dionysius withdrew into the castle and continued seeking provisions and peace. In Greece, Alexander of Pherae was murdered by his wife and two brothers, while Philip subdued the Thessalian tyrants and restored the cities to liberty.

l: Dion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dion sailed from Zacynthus to Minoa in Sicily with two ships and a thousand mercenaries, then gathered support from several Sicilian communities and amassed an army. He distributed arms to the Syracusans, was chosen general with Megacles, entered Syracuse, and was credited with restoring liberty. During the battle at the wall, he broke the mercenaries, was wounded in the right arm, and was rescued by the Syracusans before defeating the enemy.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dionysius had disarmed many Syracusans and was away in Adria when Dion entered Syracuse. He later returned, pretended to negotiate peace and restore democracy, then attacked the wall from sea to sea. After being defeated, he withdrew his foreign forces into the castle, honored his dead soldiers, and continued to control the sea while seeking provisions.

l: Alexander of Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Alexander of Pherae was murdered by his wife, who was a Theban, and by his two brothers, Lycophron and Tisiphonus. His killers were initially praised but then established their own rule with foreign soldiers and force.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Philip, king of Macedon, assisted the Aleuadae against the tyrants in Thessaly. He subdued the tyrants, restored the cities to liberty, and gained the lasting friendship and alliance of the Thessalians.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Syracusans, many of whom had been disarmed by Dionysius, joined Dion when he arrived. They chose Dion and Megacles as generals with absolute power, celebrated the end of their slavery, defended the wall from sea to sea, rescued the wounded Dion, and defeated the Dionysian forces.

l: Sicilians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Sicilians were the people Dion said he had come to restore to liberty. Sicilians from the midland and other communities joined his march against Dionysius.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Syracuse was entered by Dion after its citizens and surrounding inhabitants joined his cause. The city exchanged slavery for liberty, but Dionysius retained the castle in the Island and continued the conflict from there.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Sicily was where Dion landed to overthrow the tyranny of Dionysius. He traveled through its territories, gained support from several communities, and marched toward Syracuse.

l: wall from sea to sea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The wall from sea to sea had been built by the Syracusans near the castle in the Island. Dionysius's forces assaulted and entered it, but Dion led the Syracusans in a counterattack and defeated them there.

l: Athenian democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dionysius used the promise that he would restore democracy as a device to persuade the Syracusans to accept peace. His proposal was deceptive, and he attacked while the Syracusans were neglecting their guards.

l: tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dion came to Sicily to put down the tyranny of Dionysius. The Syracusans celebrated the overthrow of tyranny, although Dionysius continued resistance from the castle.

l: liberty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Syracusans believed that Dion restored their liberty after they had lived as slaves for fifty years. Philip likewise restored the Thessalian cities to liberty after subduing their tyrants.

l: peace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dionysius proposed peace through ambassadors while secretly preparing an attack. After the battle, Dion delayed negotiations and stated that peace required Dionysius to surrender his government and accept only honors.

l: Dion's liberation of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Dion's liberation of Syracuse began with his landing in Sicily, the gathering of allied forces, and his entry into the city. The Syracusans chose him as their general, celebrated the end of slavery, and later defended their freedom by defeating Dionysius at the wall.

l: battle at the wall, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The battle at the wall began when Dionysius's forces attacked the wall from sea to sea during a supposed truce. Dion broke the mercenaries but was wounded and nearly captured; the Syracusans rescued him, defeated the enemy, and forced the foreign forces into the castle.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Runaway servants and others in Italy formed a powerful community called the Brutii after capturing several cities. In Sicily, Philistus unsuccessfully invaded the Leontines and later lost a sea fight against the Syracusans, while Dionysius's castle remained under his supporters. Factional conflict and unpaid soldiers weakened Syracuse, and Nypsius's surprise attack allowed Dionysius's forces to capture and sack the city. Dion then returned with his mercenaries, defeated the attackers, relieved Syracuse, and was granted supreme authority by the people.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: A promiscuous multitude gathered in Lucania after coming from several parts of Italy. They first robbed and raided, then learned military discipline and conquered several cities.

l: Brutii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The people who captured Trojana, Arpinum, Thurium, and other cities formed themselves into a commonwealth and assumed the name of Brutii because many of them had been servants.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Sicily was the setting for the conflict between Dionysius, Dion, the Syracusans, and their allies. The fighting included an invasion of the Leontines, a sea fight, the capture and sack of Syracuse, and Dion's relief of the city.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Dionysius lost Philistus, his most valiant friend, and offered Dion first half and then all of the kingdom. He agreed to surrender the castle if he and his mercenaries could leave for Italy with their treasure, but he secretly sailed away with his household goods. His forces later recaptured Syracuse under Nypsius.

l: Philistus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Philistus transported cavalry to Syracuse and invaded the Leontines, but the Syracusans helped drive him out. Later, as Dionysius's lord-high-admiral, he fought the Syracusans at sea and was surrounded.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Syracuse was divided by factional conflict and suffered from poverty, unpaid soldiers, and military disorder. Nypsius's forces captured and sacked the city, but Dion later defeated them, extinguished the fires, repaired its defenses, and restored it.

l: Leontines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Leontines had fallen away from Dionysius and were invaded by Philistus. With help from the Syracusans, they repelled Philistus's attack.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Syracusans aided the Leontines, fought Philistus's fleet, and defeated Dionysius's forces at sea. They later rejected Dion's advice to accept Dionysius's terms, fought among themselves politically, and were defeated by Dion's mercenaries. Nypsius subsequently surprised and overran them, but Dion rescued the city.

l: Heraclides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Heraclides, Dion's admiral, was delayed in the Peloponnesus by storms and contrary winds. He eventually arrived with twenty galleys and fifteen hundred soldiers and was declared admiral by the Syracusans.

l: Dion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Dion joined Heraclides in managing the war against Dionysius. After the Syracusans rejected his advice and turned against him, he led three thousand foreign soldiers to the Leontines, defeated the Syracusans, and later returned to rescue Syracuse. The people then made him chief governor with full and absolute power, and he pardoned those who had injured him.

l: sea fight between Heraclides and Philistus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The unit does not describe a sea fight between Heraclides and Philistus. It describes Philistus fighting the Syracusans at sea, while Heraclides had previously been delayed in the Peloponnesus.

l: Philistus's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Philistus was surrounded after initially prevailing in the sea fight. To avoid captivity, disgrace, and misery, he killed himself; the victorious Syracusans dragged his mangled body through the city and left it unburied.

l: Acropolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Dionysius's castle was held by mercenaries who endured severe famine and nearly surrendered. Nypsius's arrival supplied them with provisions and enabled them to capture Syracuse, after which they retreated into the castle when Dion defeated them.

l: Syracusan factional conflict, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Syracusans were divided over whether Heraclides or Dion should hold supreme command and authority. Unpaid Peloponnesian soldiers also became a major source of disorder, and the people opposed Dion's advice concerning Dionysius's proposed departure.

l: battle between Dion's mercenaries and the Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Three thousand experienced soldiers urged Dion to abandon the Syracusans, and he eventually led them toward the Leontines. The Syracusans pursued and engaged them but were forced to retreat with many casualties. Dion nevertheless forgave them and released many prisoners without ransom.

l: Nypsius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Nypsius, a citizen of Naples and an experienced soldier, was sent by Dionysius with transport ships carrying corn and provisions. He relieved the starving garrison, encouraged it to continue fighting, and later led the night assault that captured Syracuse.

l: Syracusans' naval attack on Nypsius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Syracusans quickly manned their available galleys and attacked Nypsius's fleet while it was unloading corn and provisions. They sank some ships, captured others, and forced the remainder ashore.

l: Nypsius's night assault on Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: After the Syracusans celebrated their naval victory and neglected their guards, Nypsius sent selected men against the recently built wall at night. His soldiers found the guards asleep, climbed the wall, killed the sentinels, opened the gates, and captured the city.

l: Syracuse's capture and sack, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Nypsius's soldiers entered Syracuse, killed many people, plundered houses, took women, children, and servants captive, and set houses near the forum on fire. The Syracusans fought throughout the night, but confusion and lack of officers left the city in ruin until Dion arrived.

l: Dion's relief of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: After receiving an appeal from the distressed citizens, Dion marched swiftly from the Leontines to Syracuse. He entered the city from several places, attacked the scattered plunderers, killed more than four thousand, drove the survivors into the castle, extinguished the fires, repaired the wall, and restored the city's defenses.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Social War continued between the Athenians and the Chians, Rhodians, Coians, and Byzantines, with both sides preparing for a naval battle. Chares, Iphicrates, and Timotheus commanded the Athenian forces, but Iphicrates and Timotheus refused to fight during a storm and were fined and removed from command after Chares accused them of treason. Chares later joined Pharnabazus against the Persian king's forces and defeated them, but the Persian king's complaints and the rumored promise of Persian aid to Athens's enemies led the Athenians to make peace with the revolters, ending the war after four years. In Macedonia, Philip defeated the allied Thracians, Paeones, and Illyrians before they could assemble their forces and forced them under the Macedonian kingdom.

l: Social War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Social War was fought between the Athenians and the Chians, Rhodians, Coians, and Byzantines. It ended after four years when the Athenians and the revolters agreed to terms of peace.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Athenians sent a fleet under Chares and additional forces under Iphicrates and Timotheus against their rebellious confederates. After Chares accused Iphicrates and Timotheus of treason, they fined both men and revoked their commissions; later, fearing Persian support for their enemies, they agreed to peace.

l: Chians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Chians joined the Rhodians and Byzantines against the Athenians. They helped raise the siege of Samos, prepared to relieve Byzantium, and later agreed to peace with the Athenians.

l: Rhodians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Rhodians joined the Chians and Byzantines against the Athenians. Their forces helped raise the siege of Samos and prepare to relieve Byzantium, and they later agreed to peace.

l: Coians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Coians were among the Athenians' rebellious confederates in the Social War. The confederates later agreed to peace with the Athenians.

l: Byzantines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Byzantines joined the Chians and Rhodians against the Athenians. They were the object of the Athenian generals' planned siege, and their allies prepared to relieve them before the fleets met in the Hellespont.

l: Chares, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Chares commanded an Athenian fleet of sixty ships and held equal authority with Iphicrates and Timotheus. He wanted to fight despite the storm, accused his colleagues of treason when they refused, and later joined Pharnabazus to defeat the Persian king's troops. Pharnabazus gave him enough money to pay all his soldiers, but the Persian king's complaint helped lead the Athenians to end the Social War.

l: Iphicrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Iphicrates was sent with Timotheus to reinforce Chares and held equal command in the war against the rebellious confederates. During the storm in the Hellespont, he refused to fight; after Chares accused him of treason, the Athenians fined him and revoked his commission.

l: Timotheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Timotheus was sent with Iphicrates to reinforce Chares and held equal command against the rebellious confederates. He refused to fight during the storm, after which Chares accused him of treason and the Athenians fined him and revoked his commission.

l: Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Samos was attacked by the Chians, Rhodians, and Byzantines, who harassed its country and besieged its city by sea and land. The confederates later raised their siege to prepare to relieve Byzantium.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Athenian generals initially resolved to besiege Byzantium. The Chians and their confederates raised the siege of Samos and prepared to relieve Byzantium, leading the opposing fleets toward the Hellespont.

l: Pharnabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Pharnabazus had revolted from the Persian king and was preparing to fight the Persian lord-lieutenants with a small force. Chares joined him, and together they routed the king's troops; Pharnabazus then gave Chares enough money to pay all his soldiers.

l: Persian king, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Persian king's lord-lieutenants had an army of seventy thousand men, which Chares and Pharnabazus defeated. The Persian king complained to the Athenians about Chares, and a rumor that he would send three hundred ships to aid Athens's enemies helped cause the Athenians to seek peace.

l: peace settlement ending the Social War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Athenians decreed that they would adjust matters with the revolters after becoming frightened by the prospect of Persian assistance to their enemies. Since the revolters were equally willing to accept terms, the settlement was easily concluded and ended the Social War after four years.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: In Macedonia, the kings of Thrace, the Paeones, and the Illyrians allied against Philip because of his growing power. Philip defeated them before they could form their troops and brought them under the Macedonian kingdom.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Philip was opposed by the kings of Thrace, the Paeones, and the Illyrians, who had previously been defeated by him individually. He attacked them suddenly while they were raising their forces, broke them apart, and forced them to submit to the Macedonian kingdom.

l: Illyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Illyrians joined the kings of Thrace and the Paeones against Philip. Philip surprised the allied forces before their troops were formed and forced them to yield to the Macedonian kingdom.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Macedonians were opposed by an alliance of the kings of Thrace, the Paeones, and the Illyrians. Under Philip's leadership, they defeated the allied peoples and brought them under the Macedonian kingdom.

l: the kingdom of Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: The Macedonian kingdom expanded when Philip defeated the allied Thracians, Paeones, and Illyrians. Those peoples were obliged to yield to its rule.

l: Macedonian conquest of the three allied peoples, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. V.
s: Philip's conquest began with a sudden attack while the three allied peoples were still raising their forces and had no formed troops ready. He broke them apart and forced them to submit to the Macedonian kingdom.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Sacred War began when Philomelus and the Phocians seized the temple at Delphos after the Amphictyons condemned the Phocians for cultivating land claimed by the oracle. Philomelus defeated the Locrians, fortified Delphos, destroyed records of the Amphictyonic decrees, and sought support from Athens, Lacedaemon, and other Greek cities. The Boeotians and Locrians opposed him in defense of the oracle. The unit also recounts the reported discovery of the Delphic oracle, the origin of the tripod, and Philomelus's coercion of Pythia into giving an ambiguous prophecy.

l: Sacred War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Sacred War began after Philomelus seized the temple at Delphos and continued for nine years. The conflict opposed the Phocians and their allies, including the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, to the Boeotians, Locrians, and others who defended the oracle.

l: Philomelus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Philomelus persuaded the Phocians to resist the Amphictyonic decree and was appointed their sole and absolute general. With financial support from Archidamus, he raised an army, seized the temple at Delphos, defeated the Locrians, destroyed records of the Amphictyonic decrees, and sought alliances throughout Greece. He forced Pythia to ascend the tripod and interpreted her answer as permission to do what he pleased.

l: Phocians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Phocians were condemned by the Amphictyons to pay many talents because they had cultivated land at Cirrha claimed by the oracle. They appointed Philomelus as their absolute general and supplied many of his soldiers, while other Phocians were recruited into his army.

l: Delphi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Delphos was the site of the temple and oracle seized by Philomelus. Philomelus fortified the place, controlled its approaches, and made it the base for his operations against the Locrians.

l: oracle at Delphi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Philomelus attacked and seized the temple at Delphos after killing the Thracidae who opposed him. He claimed that he had taken it to recover an ancient Phocian right of custody and patronage rather than to commit sacrilege.

l: oracle of Delphos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Oracle at Delphos was claimed by the Phocians as an institution formerly under their ancestors' power and protection. Its possession became the central issue of the Sacred War, and the Boeotians, Locrians, and others took up arms to defend it.

l: Amphictyons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Amphictyons condemned the Phocians and Lacedaemonians to pay fines, and they ordered that the Phocian lands be confiscated and devoted to the deity if payment was not made. Their decree was approved by the Greeks and became the immediate cause of the Phocian resistance.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Lacedaemonians had previously been condemned by the Amphictyons for seizing Cadmea. Archidamus privately supported Philomelus's opposition to the Amphictyonic decrees by supplying money and mercenary soldiers, and the Lacedaemonians later joined the confederacy supporting the Phocians.

l: Pythia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Pythia was the prophetess who delivered answers from the tripod. Philomelus forced her to ascend it, and after she first said that the custom of the country did not permit this, she answered that it was lawful for him to do what he pleased.

l: Locrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Locrians marched against Philomelus after he seized the temple but were defeated near Delphos. Philomelus later invaded and wasted their country, fought them again, and forced them to exchange the bodies of the dead.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Boeotians resolved to relieve the temple and raised an army against Philomelus. They joined the Locrians and others in opposing the Phocians in defense of the oracle.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Athenians joined the confederacy supporting Philomelus after his ambassadors explained that he sought to recover the temple's ancient patronage rather than commit sacrilege. They promised assistance or neutrality against those who attacked the Phocians.

l: tripod, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The tripod was an apparatus with three feet on which the prophetess sat to receive inspiration and safely deliver the oracle's answers. Its form was said to explain the shape of later brass tripods.

l: Amphictyonic decrees, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Amphictyonic decrees condemned the Phocians and Lacedaemonians and threatened the Phocian land with confiscation and dedication to the deity. After defeating the Locrians, Philomelus cut the decrees from the pillars and destroyed the records concerning those condemned.

l: prophecy and divination, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: People near the chasm at Delphos were said to become inspired and speak about future events. Philomelus used Pythia's coerced answer and an omen involving an eagle and temple pigeons as encouragement for his campaign.

l: discovery of the Delphic oracle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The oracle was reportedly discovered when goats near a chasm began leaping, dancing, and making unusual noises, and a shepherd experienced the same prophetic inspiration after looking down. Because people sometimes fell into the chasm, the inhabitants appointed a woman to deliver the answers from a tripod.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Philomelus raised Phocian forces, defeated the Locrians at the Rocks of Phaedra, and later used the sacred treasures to recruit mercenaries for the Phocian war. The Boeotians, Thessalians, Locrians, and other allies opposed the Phocians, while the Athenians and Lacedaemonians supported them. Philomelus was defeated by the Boeotians and killed himself by leaping from a precipice, after which Onomarchus became general. Onomarchus renewed the war, achieved several successes, and was ultimately defeated and killed by Philip of Macedon in Thessaly.

l: Philomelus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Philomelus raised an army from the best of the Phocians and hired many soldiers. He defeated the Locrians at the Rocks of Phaedra, later rifled Apollo's temple to pay additional mercenaries, and was defeated by the Boeotians. After being driven to a precipice, he threw himself from the rock.

l: Onomarchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Onomarchus succeeded Philomelus as general of the Phocians and persuaded them to renew the war. He recruited mercenaries, distributed coined money, bribed or intimidated allies and opponents, and captured several cities. He defeated Philip of Macedon in two battles, but was later defeated and killed in Thessaly.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Philip of Macedon took Methone, destroyed it, and forced surrounding communities to submit. He later entered Thessaly, was twice defeated by Onomarchus, but returned with Thessalian support and defeated the Phocians. He captured Onomarchus and caused the other Phocian prisoners to be thrown into the sea.

l: Locrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Locrians fought Philomelus at the Rocks of Phaedra and were routed, with many killed and many taken prisoner. They later sought assistance from Thebes against the Phocians and joined the Boeotians in opposing them.

l: Phocians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Phocians supported Philomelus and Onomarchus in the war over Apollo's temple and the sacred treasures. Their forces won several engagements but suffered major defeats against the Boeotians and Philip of Macedon. After Onomarchus was killed, Phayllus became their general and rebuilt their forces.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Boeotians joined the war against the Phocians out of religious concern and support for the Amphictyonic decrees. They defeated the Phocians in a battle in rough country and later defeated Onomarchus near Chaeronea. They also sent Pammenes with an army to assist Artabazus in Asia.

l: Thessalians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Thessalians joined the forces supporting Apollo's temple and fought the Phocians at Argola, where they were defeated. Onomarchus later bribed them to remain neutral, but they subsequently joined Philip of Macedon and helped him defeat the Phocians in Thessaly.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Lacedaemonians supported the Phocians because the Thebans had prosecuted them before the Amphictyons and imposed fines over Phoebidas's seizure of Cadmea. They used the Phocian cause as a means of opposing the Amphictyonic sentence and sought influence over the temple.

l: Amphictyons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Amphictyons decreed war against the Phocians for sacrilege and violation of Apollo's temple treasures. They also condemned the Lacedaemonians to heavy fines and declared that mercenaries who fought with the Phocians should be put to death.

l: mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Mercenaries formed a substantial part of the Phocian army because Philomelus and Onomarchus offered unusually high pay from the sacred treasures. Boeotian forces killed captured Phocian mercenaries, prompting retaliation by the Phocian soldiers. More than six thousand Phocians and mercenaries were killed in the battle in which Onomarchus died.

l: Phocian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Phocian war began after the Amphictyons decreed war against the Phocians for sacrilege. It involved the Phocians, Boeotians, Locrians, Thessalians, and other Greek allies, and continued through the defeats and deaths of Philomelus and Onomarchus.

l: Locris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Locris was the scene of fighting between the Phocians and their opponents. Philomelus marched there with more than ten thousand soldiers, defeated the Locrians and Boeotians in a cavalry engagement, and later fought the Thessalians at Argola.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Thebes was asked by the Locrians to provide assistance against the Phocians. The Thebans prosecuted the Lacedaemonians before the Amphictyons, fought against Onomarchus, and sent Pammenes with five thousand men to assist Artabazus in Asia.

l: Delphi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Delphi was the location of Apollo's temple and the sacred treasures at the center of the conflict. The Phocians returned there after Philomelus's death and held a general council to decide whether to renew the war.

l: oracle of Delphos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Apollo's temple contained the sacred treasures that Philomelus initially avoided using but later rifled to finance the Phocian war. The Amphictyons treated the seizure of its treasures as sacrilege.

l: Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Thessaly became a major theater of the war between Philip of Macedon and the Phocians. Onomarchus defeated Philip there twice, but Philip later returned with Thessalian support and defeated and killed him.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Macedonia was Philip of Macedon's base. After an initial withdrawal there following defeats by Onomarchus, Philip marched again from Macedonia into Thessaly and eventually defeated the Phocian army.

l: Methone, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: Methone was besieged and captured by Philip of Macedon after Philip learned that its citizens intended to surrender it to his enemies. Its inhabitants were allowed to leave with their clothes, and Philip razed the city and divided its territory among the Macedonians.

l: battle at Phaedra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: At the battle at Phaedra, Philomelus defeated the Locrians. Many Locrians were killed, many were taken prisoner, and some were forced to leap from the rocks.

l: battle between the Boeotians and Phocians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: In the battle between the Boeotians and Phocians in rough and wooded country, the Boeotians overcame the Phocians by superior numbers. Many Phocians and mercenaries were killed during the defeat and pursuit, and Philomelus took his own life.

l: sacrilege at Delphi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Phocian sacrilege consisted of violating Apollo's temple and using its sacred treasures to finance the war. The Amphictyons condemned the Phocians for it, and Philomelus and many of his followers were treated as sacrilegious persons.

l: Amphictyonic decrees, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Amphictyonic decrees condemned the Phocians and ordered war against them. They also provided the basis for condemning captured mercenaries to death and for imposing heavy fines on the Lacedaemonians.

l: sacred treasures, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The sacred treasures were initially left untouched by Philomelus, who financed his soldiers from the estates of leading Delphians. He later rifled the treasures to offer higher pay to mercenaries, enabling him to assemble a large army.

l: Phocian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VII.
s: The Phocian army was formed from Phocian troops and large numbers of foreign mercenaries paid from the sacred treasures. It won several early engagements under Philomelus and Onomarchus but suffered severe losses against the Boeotians and Philip of Macedon.
